background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Well, you know, unfortunately, all that can happen is a political decision. The party has got to get out of the business of culture wars and get back into the business of giving people hope and opportunity and actually making the case for what we believe instead of thinking we can do that through power and, you know, all caps tweets.

background.text: I CHARACTERIZE THIS AS A COUP ATTEMPT AND, YOU KNOW, THE GOOD THING IN THIS COUNTRY, THE GUARDRAILS OF THE CONSTITUTION ARE GOING TO HOLD, THEY WILL HOLD, BUT ONE THING THIS DOES SHOW US IS THE FRAGILITY OF DEMOCRACY AND WHEN YOU HAVE PEOPLE STORMING A GOVERNMENT BUILDING SAYING THINGS LIKE 1776, A FEW PEOPLE WITH CONFEDERATE FLAGS COME AND OCCUPY THE BUILDING, YOU SEE GUNS DRAWN IN THE PEOPLE'S CHAMBER, YOU KNOW, WHERE THIS DEBATE IS SUPPOSED TO HAPPEN AND YOU SEE A PRESIDENT NON-REPENTANCE ON SOCIAL MEDIA, IT'S ABSOLUTELY A COUP ATTEMPT. background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: I'm sure you've seen the photograph of the security officers in the chamber with their guns drawn, pointed at the broken window of that famous door that we all see the president walk through for the State of the Union that you walk through every day as a part of your job. background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: investigation? Did it feel personal to you? I mean, you had been there on on January six, I think, did it feel personal?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: The investigation felt—it felt fairly personal to me, because not only had I actually been there during the attack and, you know, felt that threat, I had been a target of many of the conspiracies or the conspiracy theorists that, you know, called me a certain term and said that, you know, I was enabling, in essence, the destruction or the stealing of the election, the destruction of democracy. And so I knew that without accountability, at least verbal accountability or written accountability— not speaking yet about the federal department—without that, I mean, who knew what future history would record about this? And I knew it was essential not just for, you know, vindication in terms of what I was saying, but in vindication for the country and to defend the democracy.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: What was the most important thing that you thought the committee needed to do? Because, you know, one thing a lot of people said was we saw what happened on January 6th. We saw what the president had said. We've seen the tweets. We we'd seen the video. What was the point of the committee for you?

ground_truth: Well, besides getting to actual accountability, and I think, I mean, today I believe that this federal investigation would not have happened without the committee. But I think the most important thing is people got channelized on the day of January 6th. You know, what was January 6th? It was an attack on the government building. That became the story. I think the bigger story is not really that. January 6th was a symptom. The bigger story is everything that happened prior, and even, frankly, some of the denialism that's happened after. But everything prior, you think of, you know, the former president telling the federal department to just say the election was corrupt, right, and then leave the rest to us. We'll exploit that doubt you create, basically, or doing nothing for 187 minutes. That's what I think was most important, was to broaden America's view from being a really bad day to a really bad problem. That we have to address, and I think we were able to do that, to widen that lens.
